title: Richard Stallman's GNU Manifesto and the Invention of Copyleft (1985)
explainer: After a dispute in which he could no longer get access to improvements made to a Lisp interpreter he had shared, Richard Stallman published the GNU Manifesto in March 1985 and wrote the first 'copyleft' license, inverting ordinary copyright so that derivative works were required to stay free rather than become proprietary. The term 'copyleft' itself started as a joke on a letter he received ('Copyleft — all rights reversed'), which he then turned into enforceable license language. This is the direct origin of the licensing logic behind the GPL and every other copyleft license a contributor will run into when choosing how to license a project.

title: The Open Source Definition Began as Debian's Own Packaging Rules (1997–1998)
explainer: The 'Open Source Definition,' maintained by the Open Source Initiative since its founding in February 1998, was not written from scratch — it was adapted directly from the Debian Free Software Guidelines that Bruce Perens had drafted roughly a year earlier to decide what counted as 'free' software for the Debian Linux distribution. Stripping out the Debian-specific references turned an internal packaging policy into the checklist now used to certify licenses such as MIT, Apache, and GPL as 'open source.' Knowing this lineage clarifies why open-source licensing etiquette comes down to meeting a specific, inherited set of criteria rather than a vague sense of openness.
